function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete “starter kit” you can drop into the **`nodejs-welcome`** repository.  
I’ve written the three files that you asked for (Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, GitHub‑Actions workflow) and added a short shell script that will add, commit and push the changes for you.  

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually run `git clone`, `git add`, `git commit` or `git push` from here, so you’ll need to run the script locally after cloning the repo yourself.  

---

## 1. Clone the repo (run locally)

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2. File contents

### 2.1 `Dockerfile`

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:14-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install app dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Run the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *Why this Dockerfile?*  
> * The repo is a simple Node.js app that listens on port **3000** (the default for many Express apps).  
> * Using `node:14-alpine` gives a small, production‑ready image.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install from `package-lock.json`.  

---

### 2.2 `k8s/deployment.yaml`

Create a folder called `k8s` (or any name you prefer) and put the following file inside:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: node:14-alpine   # <-- replace with your own image if you build one
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> *What this does:*  
> * Deploys two replicas of the app.  
> * Exposes the container’s port 3000 to the cluster via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80.  
> * If you later build a Docker image (e.g., `myrepo/nodejs-welcome:latest`) replace the `image:` line accordingly.  

---

### 2.3 `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout source
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: myrepo/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your own repo/tag

      - name: Image digest
        run: echo "Image pushed with digest ${{ steps.docker_build.outputs.digest }}"
```

> **Secrets required**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (or password)  
> Replace `myrepo/nodejs-welcome:latest` with whatever registry/tag you want to use.  

---

## 3. Add, commit and push (run locally)

Create a tiny helper script called `commit_and_push.sh` in the repo root:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Stage all new/changed files
git add -A

# Commit with a meaningful message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to origin/main
git push origin main
```

Make it executable:

```bash
chmod +x commit_and_push.sh
```

Run it:

```bash
./commit_and_push.sh
```

---

## 4. Verify

After the push completes, you should see:

* A new `Dockerfile` at the repo root.  
* A `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or whatever folder you chose).  
* A `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` that triggers on pushes to `main`.  

If you’re using a CI/CD platform that supports GitHub Actions, the workflow will automatically build and push the Docker image whenever you push to `main`.  

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Build locally to make sure everything works
docker build -t nodejs-welcome-test .

# Run the container
docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome-test
```

Open `http://localhost:3000` in your browser – you should see the app’s response.  

That’s it! 🎉 If you hit any snags (e.g., missing secrets, wrong image names), feel free to let me know and I’ll help tweak the files.
